Q1259987.title: Exsurge Domine
paras: Pope Leo X had authorised a large sale of indulgences, partly to pay for the rebuilding of St Peter's in Rome, and Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses against its abuses in 1517 had set off a revolt across Germany. Neither the papal legate Cardinal Cajetan at Augsburg in 1518 nor a papal bull on indulgences had made Luther retract, and at the Leipzig Debate of 1519 Johann Eck had drawn him into open rejection of papal authority. In January 1520 a commission met in Rome to examine Luther's teachings. Eck joined it halfway through, bringing the condemnations of Luther issued by the universities of Cologne and Leuven, and he pressed it towards a quick and sweeping verdict.

The commission, of some forty cardinals, theologians and canon lawyers, was divided: some feared that condemning so popular a figure was politically dangerous, the theologians wanted immediate condemnation, and the canon lawyers wanted Luther to be heard first. The compromise gave him no hearing but sixty days to recant. Instead of answering each point, the text simply listed forty-one propositions from Luther's writings, more than half from the Ninety-five Theses and their defence and much of the rest from the Leipzig Debate, and condemned them all together as heretical, scandalous, false, offensive to pious ears or misleading to simple minds. Leo X added a preface, which opens with the words Exsurge Domine ('Arise, O Lord') and calls on God to rise against a wild boar ravaging his vineyard, and issued the bull on 15 June 1520.

According to its text as Wikipedia quotes it, the bull ordered Luther's books to be burned and threatened him and his supporters, among them Andreas Karlstadt, with excommunication unless they recanted within sixty days of its publication in Saxony and the neighbouring lands. Eck took it to Germany as papal nuncio and published it with two papal legates, but bishops, universities and humanists alike denounced it; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says Eck was lucky to escape from Saxony unharmed. Luther refused to recant, attacked the papacy in new pamphlets and on 10 December 1520 publicly burned a copy of the bull at the Elster Gate in Wittenberg. On 3 January 1521 Leo X excommunicated him with the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem.

Q1425362.title: Battle of Cajamarca
paras: Francisco Pizarro, licensed by Charles V in 1529 to conquer the coast he had explored, sailed from Panama in January 1531 with three ships, 180 men and 27 horses, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He reached the Inca Empire just as Atahualpa had won a civil war against his half-brother Huáscar, whom his commanders had just captured. Atahualpa was camped outside the highland town of Cajamarca with an army that Wikipedia puts at nearly 80,000 veterans, and he let the small Spanish force come inland, apparently confident that it could do him no harm. The Spaniards entered the half-empty town on 15 November 1532. Unable either to attack such an army or to retreat safely, Pizarro planned to seize the emperor himself, as Cortés had seized Moctezuma.

On the afternoon of 16 November Atahualpa came into the town's great square, carried on a litter lined with parrot feathers and plated with gold and silver, with thousands of richly dressed attendants who were unarmed or carried only ceremonial weapons; his main army stayed outside the town. The Spaniards were hidden in the buildings round the square, with horsemen in the alleys and guns in a central stone building. The friar Vicente de Valverde came out with an interpreter and called on Atahualpa to accept the Christian faith. Pizarro's secretary Francisco de Xerez, an eyewitness, says the Inca threw down the book he was handed and complained of how the Spaniards had treated his people on their march; Spanish sources differ on exactly what set off the fighting.

At the signal the guns fired and the horsemen and infantry charged out. The attendants offered almost no resistance; many died shielding the litter, and the crowd fleeing the square broke down part of its wall. Pizarro reached the litter and seized Atahualpa, receiving a cut on the hand while protecting him from his own men. The Inca army outside the town scattered. Thousands of Atahualpa's nobles, counsellors and attendants were killed; most sources say no Spaniard died.

The capture began the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire. To buy his freedom Atahualpa promised, Xerez records, to fill a room 22 feet long and 17 wide with gold up to a line half way up the wall, and twice with silver. The ransom was gathered and shared out among the conquerors, but Atahualpa was not freed: sentenced to death on a charge of treason, which the 19th-century translator Clements Markham calls a false pretext, he was baptised and then strangled at Cajamarca in 1533.

Q2091449.title: Battle of Mactan
paras: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in the service of Spain, had left Spain in 1519 to find a western route to the Spice Islands. After crossing the Pacific his fleet sighted Samar on 16 March 1521 and on 7 April reached Cebu. There Rajah Humabon accepted baptism, taking the name Carlos after the Spanish king, and became Magellan's ally; at Magellan's urging the neighbouring chiefs were told to supply the ships and to accept Christianity. On the small island of Mactan, beside the harbour where the fleet lay, the chief Lapulapu (Cilapulapu in the account of the voyage's chronicler, Antonio Pigafetta) refused to submit to Humabon or to the king of Spain. Mactan's other chief, Zula, sent Magellan a son with two goats and asked for a boatload of men to help him against Lapulapu.

Against the pleas of his officers, Magellan decided to lead the attack himself. Pigafetta writes that sixty men in corselets and helmets set out at midnight in three boats, with Humabon and twenty or thirty local boats, and reached Mactan three hours before dawn on Saturday, 27 April. Magellan offered friendship if the islanders would obey the king of Spain, recognise Humabon as their sovereign and pay tribute; they answered that they had lances of bamboo and stakes hardened in fire. Rocks kept the boats far from the shore, so at daybreak 49 men waded in up to their thighs while 11 guarded the boats. Magellan had told Humabon to stay in his boat and watch.

On the beach, Pigafetta says, more than 1,500 warriors in three divisions attacked the landing party from the front and both flanks. The musketeers and crossbowmen fired uselessly from too far off for about half an hour, and when Magellan had houses set on fire the defenders grew only more furious. Shot in the right leg with a poisoned arrow, he ordered a slow withdrawal, but most of his men fled, leaving six or eight with him; aiming at their bare legs, the islanders drove them back into knee-deep water, where they fought for more than an hour. Wounded in the arm by a bamboo spear so that he could not draw his sword, and then cut in the left leg by a large sword (probably a kampilan, according to Wikipedia), Magellan fell and was killed. Pigafetta counts eight Europeans killed with him, four Christian islanders killed by the boats' own guns, and fifteen of the enemy dead.

Lapulapu's people refused to give up Magellan's body for any amount of goods. Days later Humabon turned on his allies: Wikipedia says survivors were poisoned at a feast he gave, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that he seized and murdered several leaders, among them Juan Serrano, one of the two commanders chosen to replace Magellan. The survivors burned one of their three ships and left the Philippines; the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, reached Spain in 1522, completing the first voyage around the world. In the Philippines the battle is remembered as the first victory of a native Filipino over Spanish forces, and Lapulapu as the country's first national hero; in 2017, 27 April was declared Lapulapu Day.

Q2558706.title: Francis Drake's circumnavigation
Q2558706.place: Plymouth, England, and around the world
paras: Francis Drake was an English seaman who had sailed with his kinsman John Hawkins against the Spanish at San Juan de Ulúa in the Caribbean and had raided Spanish Panama in 1572–1573, when he first saw the Pacific. Protestant England did not accept the Spanish and Portuguese division of the world under the Treaty of Tordesillas, and relations between Queen Elizabeth I and Philip II of Spain were deteriorating. With the queen's backing Drake proposed a voyage through the Strait of Magellan into the Pacific, where no Englishman had yet sailed. Officially a voyage of discovery, it was in effect a covert raiding expedition against Spain's Pacific coast.

Five small ships with about 164 men (166 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica) left Plymouth in November 1577 but were driven back by a storm, and sailed again on 13 December. At Port St Julian in Patagonia Drake had Thomas Doughty, one of his company, tried and beheaded for plotting against him. He renamed his flagship, the Pelican, the Golden Hind and entered the Strait of Magellan in August 1578, but storms in the Pacific scattered the fleet: the Marigold was lost, presumably with all hands, and the Elizabeth under John Wynter returned to England, leaving the Golden Hind alone.

Drake sailed up the coast of Chile and Peru, plundering Spanish towns and ships, and on 1 March 1579 captured the treasure ship Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, laden with silver. To avoid the Spanish, who were now hunting him, he sailed north in search of a passage back to the Atlantic, then landed in what is now northern California to repair his ship; he named the land New Albion and claimed it for Elizabeth. In late July 1579 he set out across the Pacific, reached the Moluccas, where the sultan of Ternate received him well and he traded for about ten tonnes of spices, mostly cloves; after the ship struck a rock off Celebes and was got off again, he went on to Java, rounded the Cape of Good Hope in June 1580 and reached Plymouth on 26 September 1580 with 59 men and a rich cargo of spices and Spanish treasure.

Drake was the first Englishman to sail round the world and the first captain since Magellan's expedition to complete a circumnavigation in his own ship. After some hesitation, for fear of trouble with Spain, the queen knighted him aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford on 4 April 1581, to the anger of Philip II, who regarded him as a pirate. The voyage was one of the causes of the Anglo-Spanish War of 1585–1604, and Spain answered Drake's entry into the Pacific by trying to colonise the Strait of Magellan to close it.

Q371558.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
paras: John Calvin, a young French scholar trained in law and classics, became a Protestant around 1533, at a time when the reform movement was persecuted in France, and had to go into hiding. He began the studies that led to his great book while staying at Angoulême in 1534, and in 1535 took refuge in Basel, then a centre of Protestant learning. King Francis I, who was persecuting Protestants at home but wanted to stay on good terms with the Lutheran princes of Germany against Charles V, had his envoys explain that he was punishing only Anabaptists and other enemies of all civil government. Calvin was indignant at this slur on the French reformers and rushed his work into print.

The Institutes of the Christian Religion (Institutio Christianae Religionis) was published in Latin at Basel in March 1536, so that it could reach educated readers in every country. It opened with a letter to Francis I asking him to give the Protestants a hearing instead of persecuting them, and presenting the book as their confession of faith. The first edition was a short manual in six chapters, following the traditional order of religious teaching: the Law (the Ten Commandments), faith (the Apostles' Creed), prayer and the sacraments, followed by chapters on the 'false sacraments' and on Christian liberty, church power and civil government. It drew on Luther for faith and the sacraments and on Martin Bucer of Strasbourg for predestination. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that Calvin was only twenty-six when it appeared.

The book was an immediate success, and Calvin, who soon afterwards began his ministry in Geneva, kept enlarging it. A much larger Latin edition appeared in 1539 and further ones in 1543 and 1550, and he also translated it into French: Wikipedia dates the first French edition to 1541, while the Britannica says the earliest known one is of 1540. The final Latin edition of 1559, which scholars treat as the authoritative text, is 80% larger than the one before it, yet Calvin's essential ideas did not change. The Institutes became the core statement of the doctrine of the Reformed churches, usually called Calvinism, and one of the most influential works of Protestant theology.

Q593267.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
paras: Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Mexica (Aztecs) in Lake Texcoco, fell after a two-year struggle with the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés. Cortés had landed on the Gulf coast in April 1519 with 508 soldiers, 100 sailors and 14 small cannon, and won allies among peoples who resented Aztec rule, above all the Tlaxcalans. Received in Tenochtitlan, he made the emperor Moctezuma his prisoner. When he left the city to defeat a Spanish force sent from Cuba to arrest him, his lieutenant Pedro de Alvarado provoked a rising. Moctezuma died, and the Spaniards fought their way out of the city at night, an escape remembered as La Noche Triste; by the time they reached Tlaxcala, Wikipedia says, they had lost more than 860 Spanish soldiers and over a thousand Tlaxcalans. On the way they beat a large Aztec army at Otumba, on 7 July 1520 according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.

While Cortés rebuilt his forces, a smallpox epidemic, to which the Spaniards were largely immune, swept the Valley of Mexico and killed many Aztec leaders; Cuauhtémoc became emperor in February 1521. Cortés had thirteen brigantines built in pieces at Tlaxcala and launched on the lake from Texcoco, gathered reinforcements and tens of thousands of native warriors, and won over the lakeside towns. On 22 May 1521 three columns under Alvarado, Cristóbal de Olid and Gonzalo de Sandoval took up positions at the heads of the causeways, cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec that brought much of the city's water, and the brigantines scattered the Aztec canoe fleet.

The siege lasted about three months. The Aztecs fought street by street; in one counter-attack Cortés was wounded and almost captured, and sixty-five Spaniards were taken alive and sacrificed in sight of their comrades. Cortés answered by razing each district he took and using the rubble to fill the canals, so that his cavalry and infantry could advance in formation, while the blockade starved the city: its people ate wood and leather and drank brackish water, and disease spread. The attackers finally reached the market square of Tlatelolco. Cuauhtémoc tried to escape by canoe but was captured by Sandoval's brigantines, and the Aztecs surrendered on 13 August 1521, the date also given by the Britannica.

The fall of the city destroyed the Aztec state and was a critical stage in Spain's colonisation of the Americas. Wikipedia gives estimates of 100,000 to 240,000 killed in the campaign as a whole, warriors and civilians together; almost all the Aztec nobility died, and Spain's native allies, mainly the Tlaxcalans, went on killing and looting after the surrender.

Q645920.title: Protestation at Speyer
paras: Martin Luther had been placed under the ban of the Holy Roman Empire by the Edict of Worms in 1521, but the edict was not enforced everywhere. In 1526 the first Diet of Speyer resolved that, until a church council met, each state should conduct its religious affairs as it hoped to answer for them to God and the emperor, and the Lutheran princes took this as licence to organise their own territorial churches. In 1529 Emperor Charles V, at war with France, called a second diet at Speyer and was represented by his brother Ferdinand. Ferdinand announced that the emperor annulled the 1526 decision; according to Wikipedia's account of his declarations, further innovations were forbidden until a council, the Mass was to be refused to no one, and neither those who rejected the real presence of Christ in the sacrament nor the Anabaptists were to be tolerated.

The Catholic majority of the diet accepted the revocation on 19 April 1529 and told the evangelical estates to yield to it. The evangelical princes left the hall, and when they returned Ferdinand refused to hear them, so their objection was read out: they would keep to the decision of 1526 and would not be bound by the majority in matters of faith. On 20 April they presented a formal Letter of Protestation, which Ferdinand refused to accept; it was printed and published instead. Its signers were Elector John of Saxony, Margrave George of Brandenburg-Ansbach, Duke Ernest of Brunswick-Lüneburg, Landgrave Philip of Hesse and Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt, joined by representatives of 14 imperial free cities, among them Strasbourg and Ulm.

When the diet's decree was read again at its last sitting on 24 April without mention of the protest, the princes' councillors and the cities' agents drew up a formal appeal on 25 April and sent it to the emperor by an embassy. From this protest the reformers took the name Protestants, and the event is often counted as the birth of Protestantism. As the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica observes, a minority could hold to such a protest only if it was ready to defend itself by force, and three days after the protest was read many of the protesting cities and states made a secret treaty, while Philip of Hesse began to work for a general union of the evangelical states.

Q661327.title: Battle of Mühlberg
Q661327.place: Mühlberg on the Elbe, Saxony, Germany
paras: The battle was the decisive clash of the Schmalkaldic War between Emperor Charles V and the Schmalkaldic League, the defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and cities led by Elector John Frederick of Saxony and Landgrave Philip of Hesse. For years Charles had tolerated the league while he fought France and the Ottomans, but the Treaty of Crépy with France in 1544 freed his hands. The war began in 1546 when Maurice of Saxony, a Protestant cousin and rival of John Frederick who had refused to join the league, invaded the elector's lands with the help of Charles's brother Ferdinand. John Frederick drove him back, but the emperor joined the war, occupied Ulm and Württemberg, forced the Elector Palatine to submit, and in spring 1547 marched into Saxony.

John Frederick had sent much of his army to Bohemia, hoping for a Protestant rising there, and was withdrawing north towards his fortress of Wittenberg. He camped at Mühlberg, leaving only a few guards on the Elbe, which he thought too wide for the imperial army to cross quickly. Charles, so ill with gout that he was carried in a litter, reached the river on the evening of 23 April and, against his generals' advice, decided to attack. At dawn on 24 April, under cover of fog, Spanish and Italian veterans swam the river and overcame the Saxon guards; a local farmer showed the Duke of Alba's men a ford, and the cavalry crossed by a pontoon bridge that the Saxons had failed to destroy.

Taken by surprise, the elector drew up his army along the edge of a forest. The imperial cavalry under Alba and Maurice broke the Saxon wings, and the infantry tercios in the centre drove the Protestants back into the forest. John Frederick fought bravely but was wounded in the face and captured. Wikipedia puts the Saxon losses at 2,000 to 3,000 men, with nearly all their artillery and banners taken, against about fifty imperial dead.

The victory decided the war in the emperor's favour, and the league was dissolved. Charles spared John Frederick's life in exchange for the surrender of Wittenberg, but kept him prisoner and transferred his electoral title to Maurice; Philip of Hesse submitted soon afterwards. The success did not last: within a few years a new conflict broke out, and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555 allowed each ruler to choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism.

Q688998.title: Leipzig Debate
paras: Two years after Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, the quarrel had become a contest between named champions. Johann Eck, professor of theology at Ingolstadt and a famous debater, had in 1518 circulated a privately written attack, the Obelisci, branding Luther a Hussite, a follower of Jan Hus, whose teachings the Council of Constance had condemned. Andreas Karlstadt, dean of the theology faculty at Wittenberg, took up Luther's defence, answered Eck in a long series of theses and challenged him to a public debate. Eck accepted, and the debate was held in June and July 1519 in the Pleissenburg castle at Leipzig, in the presence of Duke George of Saxony, himself an opponent of Luther.

According to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, Eck first debated Karlstadt on 27 and 28 June and 1 and 3 July on grace, free will and good works. From 4 to 14 July he faced Luther, and the subject widened to purgatory, indulgences, penance and, above all, the authority of the pope. Eck's aim was to push Luther into a statement that would let his opponents identify him with Hus, and he succeeded: Luther conceded that some of Hus's opinions were true and declared himself against the papacy.

The judges gave no verdict, but the general impression, says the Britannica, was that Eck had won, and Luther went back to Wittenberg depressed. Yet the debate made Luther see that his protest struck at the centre of the church's system, not at an abuse on its edge. His published account rallied support in Germany, and in 1520 he wrote his three great reforming treatises. Eck, meanwhile, went to Rome, and the papal bull Exsurge Domine of June 1520, which he helped to prepare, followed the line of his charges at Leipzig and threatened Luther with excommunication.

Q691882.title: Münster rebellion
paras: The Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and baptised adult believers again, and some of them expected the end of the world to be near. After the Peasants' War of 1524–1525 their most radical wing made a new attempt to set up a kingdom of the saints at Münster in Westphalia, a city of the prince-bishopric of Münster in the Holy Roman Empire. There the Lutheran preacher Bernhard Rothmann, backed by the wealthy wool merchant Bernhard Knipperdolling, moved from attacking Catholicism to preaching the equality of all believers, including in property. Followers of Jan Matthys, a baker from Haarlem, among them the tailor Jan Bockelson (John of Leiden), declared Münster the New Jerusalem; from 5 January 1534 adult baptism spread quickly, and in February the Anabaptists won control of the city council and made Knipperdolling mayor.

Many Lutherans left and Anabaptists arrived from outside. Rebaptism was made compulsory, churches and monasteries were stripped of images, and property was declared common. The expelled bishop, Franz von Waldeck, laid siege to the city. At Easter 1534 Matthys, who had prophesied God's judgement for that day and saw himself as a second Gideon, went out against the besiegers with a handful of men and was killed with all of them: twelve followers according to Wikipedia, thirty according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.

John of Leiden took his place, claimed visions from heaven, proclaimed himself the successor of King David with royal honours and absolute power, and made polygamy legal. Wikipedia says he took sixteen wives, the Britannica four; both report that he beheaded one of them in the market place, though Wikipedia notes that this may have been attributed to him falsely. As the siege dragged on, most of the people starved. After a long resistance the besiegers took the city on 24 June 1535. In January 1536 John of Leiden, Knipperdolling and Bernhard Krechting were tortured and executed in the market place, and their bodies were hung in cages from the tower of St Lambert's Church, where the cages still hang.

Münster was the turning point of the Anabaptist movement: after it, Catholic and Lutheran rulers alike suppressed the Anabaptists harshly, and they never again had political weight. The peaceful Anabaptists who followed Menno Simons, the Mennonites, rejected the doctrines of the Münster radicals.

cp04-16.title: First circumnavigation completed (Magellan–Elcano expedition)
paras: The expedition was a Spanish venture, paid for mostly by King Charles I, to reach the Moluccas, the Spice Islands, by sailing west, since the eastern route around Africa belonged to Portugal under the Treaty of Tordesillas. Its commander, the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan, left Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 20 September 1519 with five ships and about 270 men. The fleet passed through the strait at the tip of South America that now bears his name late in 1520 and crossed the Pacific in 98 days, the crews eating ox-hides, sawdust and rats as scurvy spread.

Magellan was killed in a fight on Mactan in the Philippines on 27 April 1521, and soon afterwards many of his officers were murdered on Cebu. The survivors burned one ship and reached Tidore in the Moluccas in November 1521, where they loaded cloves. The flagship Trinidad was found to be leaking and stayed behind (it was later captured by the Portuguese), so on 21 December 1521 the Victoria, commanded by the Spanish navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano, set out for Spain alone by the Portuguese route across the Indian Ocean.

The homeward voyage was a race against hunger. With only rice to eat, the Victoria rounded the Cape of Good Hope on 6 May 1522 after weeks of storms. By 9 July, when Elcano put into the Portuguese Cape Verde Islands for food, twenty men had died according to Wikipedia (twenty-one, counting Europeans and Moluccans, according to the voyage's chronicler Antonio Pigafetta). There the crew discovered that their carefully kept log was a day behind the islanders' calendar, the day gained by sailing round the world westward. When the Portuguese learned where the ship had been, they seized thirteen men ashore and the Victoria fled.

On Saturday 6 September 1522 the Victoria entered the bay of Sanlúcar with 18 men, most of them sick, almost three years after setting out; two days later they anchored at Seville and went barefoot with candles to give thanks at its shrines. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives 31 men as returning with Elcano. The men held in Cape Verde were later released, and a few survivors of the Trinidad came home years later. The voyage was the first circumnavigation of the Earth and the first European crossing of the Pacific, and it showed both the vastness of that ocean and that the world could be sailed round by a western sea route.

cp04-18.title: Jacques Cartier explores the Gulf of St. Lawrence
cp04-18.place: Gulf of St. Lawrence (Newfoundland, Gaspé), Canada
paras: Jacques Cartier was a navigator from Saint-Malo in Brittany. Introduced to King Francis I by the bishop of Saint-Malo, Jean Le Veneur, he was commissioned to look for a western passage to the riches of Asia and for lands said to hold gold. France had already sent Giovanni da Verrazzano to explore the North American coast in 1524. Cartier sailed from Saint-Malo on 20 April 1534 with two ships and, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, sixty-one men.

He reached Newfoundland on 10 May after twenty days at sea and entered the Strait of Belle Isle. Turning south, he followed the west coast of Newfoundland into the Gulf of St. Lawrence, passed the Bird Rocks, where his crew killed about 1,000 birds, most of them great auks, and named Brion Island after Admiral Chabot. He took the Magdalen Islands and Prince Edward Island for the mainland, and was disappointed to find that Chaleur Bay was not a strait. On its north shore he met and traded briefly with local people, probably Mi'kmaq.

In Gaspé Bay he met a party of St. Lawrence Iroquoians from the Quebec region. There, on 24 July, he set up a tall cross inscribed 'Long live the King of France', claiming the land for Francis I, and he took two sons of their chief Donnacona back with him; Wikipedia describes this as a kidnapping to which the chief at last consented on condition that they return with goods to trade. He then coasted round Anticosti Island, mistaking the channel to the north of it for a bay, and on finding it a council decided to leave its exploration to the next year. He left the Gulf through the Strait of Belle Isle on 15 August and reached Saint-Malo on 5 September 1534, convinced that he had reached an Asian land.

The voyage opened the way for French claims in North America. In 1535 Cartier returned with three ships, 110 men and his two captives, who guided him up the St. Lawrence to Donnacona's town of Stadacona and on to Hochelaga, the site of Montreal, which he reached on 2 October 1535. The captives' word for a village, kanata, gave Canada its name.

cp05-09.title: Schmalkaldic League formed
paras: Soon after the start of the Reformation, the Lutheran princes and cities of the Holy Roman Empire looked for protection against their Catholic emperor, Charles V. At the town of Schmalkalden they formally concluded a defensive alliance on 27 February 1531, pledging to defend one another if the emperor attacked their lands. Its leaders were Landgrave Philip of Hesse and the house of Saxony: the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913 lists Elector John of Saxony and his son John Frederick among the parties, while Wikipedia names John Frederick as co-founder with Philip. Other founding members included Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt, dukes of Brunswick, the counts of Mansfeld and cities such as Strasbourg, Ulm, Constance, Magdeburg and Bremen. At Saxony's insistence, members had to accept the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession.

According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, the members bound themselves for six years to treat an attack on any one of them, on account of religion or on any other pretext, as an attack on all. Saxony and Hesse were made its military commanders, and the league's forces were fixed at 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry. It sought foreign allies, among them France, and later Denmark. In December 1535 it was renewed for ten years and opened to all who accepted the Augsburg Confession; Württemberg, Pomerania, Anhalt and cities such as Augsburg and Frankfurt joined.

Charles V was tied down for years by wars with France and the Ottoman Empire, and the threat from the Ottomans led his brother Ferdinand to grant the Protestants a religious peace at Nuremberg in July 1532. Under the league's protection its members spread Lutheranism across northern Germany, confiscating church lands and expelling bishops; in 1542 they drove the Catholic Duke Henry out of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Once Charles had made peace with France he turned on the league. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 his forces routed the league's army at Mühlberg on 24 April 1547 and captured John Frederick, and the league was dissolved. The defeat proved temporary: a Protestant victory in 1552 led to the Peace of Passau and three years later to the Peace of Augsburg, which gave Lutheranism official status in the Empire.

cp05-13.title: Society of Jesus approved
paras: The Society of Jesus grew from a group of students at the University of Paris around Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque from Spain and a former soldier. On 15 August 1534 Ignatius and six companions, among them Francis Xavier, Peter Faber, Diego Laínez and Simão Rodrigues, met in a crypt at Montmartre and vowed themselves to poverty and chastity (Wikipedia adds obedience; the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913 names only poverty and chastity, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates their vow to obey an elected superior to 1539). They hoped to go to the Holy Land, but war made the journey impossible. In 1537 they went to Italy, where Pope Paul III allowed them to be ordained priests, and they gave themselves to preaching and charitable work. When the hope of Jerusalem was finally given up, they agreed on a common rule and the name Company of Jesus.

Ignatius, Faber and Laínez then offered their services to the pope in Rome. Paul III received them well, but their plan met strong opposition: a commission of cardinals had just reported that the existing religious orders had decayed so badly that they should all be abolished, and Cardinal Guidiccioni, who examined the draft, wanted no new orders. Ignatius's idea of priests who would live in the world, with no distinctive habit or enclosure, also broke with tradition. In 1539 the companions bound themselves to obey a superior elected from among them and added a special vow of obedience to the pope for missions. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits King John III of Portugal, who wanted Jesuits for Portugal and its Indian possessions, with helping to change Guidiccioni's mind.

On 27 September 1540 Paul III confirmed the new society with the bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae, which, as the Britannica quotes it, set out Ignatius's formula: the society existed to spread the faith by preaching, the Spiritual Exercises, works of charity and the teaching of children and the uneducated, and all its members served under obedience to the pope. The bull limited the society to sixty members, a restriction removed, according to Wikipedia, by Julius III in 1550, but according to the Britannica by Paul III himself in 1543. Ignatius was chosen as the first superior general.

The Jesuits became an important force in the Counter-Reformation and in Catholic missions. Francis Xavier, sent to Portugal in March 1540, left Europe for the Indian mission the next year, and the society went on to found colleges and missions across Europe, Asia and the Americas.

cp18-098.title: Khanate of Khiva founded
cp18-098.place: Khwarazm (Vazir, Urgench and Khiva), Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan
paras: At the start of the 16th century Khwarazm (Khorezm), the irrigated oasis of the lower Amu Darya south of the Aral Sea, changed hands several times. It had been nominally subject to the Timurid sultan Husayn Bayqara of Khorasan until 1505, when it was taken by Muhammad Shaybani, the leader of the Uzbeks, who had overthrown Timurid rule in Transoxiana. In 1510 Shaybani was defeated and killed near Merv by Shah Ismail I, the founder of Shia Safavid Persia, and Khwarazm passed to the shah. According to the 19th-century historian Henry Howorth, who followed the chronicle of the later Khivan khan Abu'l-Ghazi, Ismail put three Persian governors over its towns: one at Urgench, the capital, one over Khiva and Hazarasp, and one at Vazir.

The Sunni townspeople and tribes resented the Shia governors. Howorth relates that the people of Vazir, urged on by a holy man named Husamuddin Katal, secretly invited Ilbars, the son of the Uzbek chief Bereke Sultan, to become their khan. The conspirators seized the town gates and massacred the Persians inside; only one escaped. Ilbars was proclaimed khan at a feast of Uzbeks and Sarts and made Vazir his residence. Three months later he defeated the Persian governor of Urgench, Sultan Kuli, outside that town and took it, and he called in kinsmen and their tribes from the Kipchak steppe, whose raids made the Persian garrisons give up Khiva and Hazarasp. Wikipedia dates the expulsion of the shah's garrison and Ilbars's accession to 1511, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the start of Uzbek rule in Khiva to 1512. Abu'l-Ghazi gives the year 911 of the Hijra, which Howorth rejects because the rising came after Shaybani's death; he suggests it may have been 921.

Ilbars and his kin were themselves Shaybanids, but of a rival line. Their dynasty, the Arabshahids or Yadigarids, was named after Arabshah and his descendant Yadigar, who had been proclaimed khan north of the Aral Sea in about 1458 (Wikipedia); Howorth adds that Ilbars's father Bereke Sultan had been hunted down and killed by Muhammad Shaybani himself. The new state was therefore a second Uzbek khanate and a rival of the Shaybanid khanate of Bukhara up the river.

From Khwarazm the Uzbeks raided Khorasan and the Turkmens, especially after Shah Ismail's death. The capital stayed at Urgench until about 1600, when a branch of the Amu Darya dried up and Arab Muhammad Khan (1602–1623) moved it to Khiva, which gave the state its later name. The khanate fought repeated wars with Bukhara, was occupied by Nader Shah of Persia in 1740–1746, came under the Qongrat dynasty and became a Russian protectorate in 1873. It lasted until 1920, when it was replaced by the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic.
